ann_82.original: Heavy daytime calling raises predicted churn through this gate; heavy evening calling lowers the daytime level at which it opens, and holding a voicemail plan raises that level. Daytime minutes enter the gate with a weight of 0.85 per sd and the gate reaches the score with a weight of 4.25. Self-probe (typical customer without a voicemail plan, through this part): the gate adds 0.00 to the log-odds at 225 day minutes, 1.41 at 250 and 4.76 at 300. With a voicemail plan (30 messages) it adds 0.00 at 275 minutes and 1.10 at 300, so the plan moves the opening point up. Evening minutes are the partner: at 200 day minutes the gate adds 0.00 with 200 evening minutes and 2.23 with 300 evening minutes. In the training data the gate is open for 626 of 4000 customers, whose observed churn rate is 42.2%; for them it adds 2.39 to the log-odds on average. Of the 1061 voicemail-plan holders, 27 have it open, against 599 of the 2939 customers without a plan. Switching the gate off lowers training AUC from 0.911 to 0.841. A Washington DC term inside the gate is small: switching it off changes predicted risk for 7 customers, by at most 1.5%. The attached formula (coefficients rounded to three significant figures) reproduces the gate to within 0.0048.
ann_82.proposed: This part acts on 626 of the 4000 training customers, mostly without a voice-mail plan, and raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves for a typical such customer from about 5% to about 35%; more evening minutes add to it mainly above 180 daytime minutes, and a voice-mail plan works against it.

ann_83.original: Customer service calls barely move predicted churn up to 2 calls and then raise it steeply: a hinge. The calls enter twice: a direct term of 1.62 per sd, and a gate (output weight 2.79) that reads the calls with a weight of -0.55 per sd and so shuts when calls are high. While the gate is open it cancels most of the direct slope; once it shuts, the direct slope acts in full. Self-probe (typical customer, through this part): the part gives -0.37 at 0 calls, -0.24 at 2, 0.39 at 3, 1.63 at 4 and 2.87 at 5 calls; whole-model predicted churn goes from 1.6% at 1 call to 9.9% at 4 and 27.4% at 5. Daytime minutes also feed the gate (0.29 per sd), so while it is open more daytime use adds to predicted churn: at 1 call, going from 180 to 280 day minutes moves this part from -0.31 to 1.21, while at 5 calls it gives 2.87 at 180 and 2.87 at 280 minutes. Oregon carries a large negative weight on the gate (-2.65 per sd) and keeps it shut: it is open for 0 of the 84 Oregon training customers. An Oregon customer with few calls therefore gets a lower prediction (1 call, typical case: 0.4% against 1.6%); this looks fitted to those 84 rows. Alaska lowers the gate slightly as well (typical case through this part: -1.16 against -0.30 for Alabama; 56 Alaska customers). In the training data the gate is shut for 1025 customers and open for 2975. The 318 customers with 4 or more calls churned at 50.0% (mean prediction 41.8%); the 3682 with 3 or fewer at 11.1% (mean prediction 11.5%). Replacing the part by its training mean lowers AUC from 0.911 to 0.840. The attached formula reproduces the part to within 0.0075.
ann_83.proposed: This part raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves as calls to customer service rise, slowly at first, then faster, more so in Oregon and at 180 daytime minutes or fewer; Oregon and Alaska lower it.

ann_84.original: This gate raises predicted churn for customers with a low daytime charge, and more so when their international charge is also low. Daytime charge enters with a weight of -0.88 per sd, so the gate shrinks as the daytime charge rises and shuts for high spenders; a second unit, which opens when the international charge is low, adds to it (weight 0.98). Self-probe (typical customer, through this part): with the typical international charge the gate adds 1.50 to the log-odds at a 20-dollar day charge, 0.55 at 30 and 0.00 at 40; with an international charge of 1 dollar it adds 2.83, 1.88 and 0.94. Sweeping the international charge alone, the part gives 2.87 at 0 dollars, 0.77 at 2 dollars and 0.49 at 2.5 dollars. International minutes pull the other way through their direct term in account_direct_terms, so for a realistic low user (3.7 minutes, 1 dollar) whole-model predicted churn is 2.2% against 1.6% for the typical customer. In the training data the gate is open for 2987 customers, adding 0.99 on average for them; the low-international-charge unit is open for 960. Its main role is as a counterweight: daytime minutes raise the service-calls gate, and this gate takes most of that rise back for low and average daytime use (see usage_and_service). Switching it off lowers training AUC from 0.911 to 0.899. The attached formula reproduces the gate to within 0.00077.

Michigan suppresses that rise: the unit is open for 0 of the 80 Michigan customers, and the part gives -0.00, -0.01 and -0.02 at those charges. Rhode Island lowers the score through an always-on unit: -0.98 at a 30-dollar day charge (82 customers). A Tennessee unit is open for every Tennessee customer (0 of the 68 have it shut) and for none elsewhere (0 non-Tennessee customers have it open); it lowers the score more as the evening charge rises: -0.13 at a 5-dollar evening charge, -0.31 at 30 dollars. Self-probe (typical case, sweep over states, through this part, with each state's training n and observed rate): Hawaii -1.95 (n 73, observed 4.1%), Vermont -1.77 (n 80, 6.2%), Colorado -1.16 (n 78, 9.0%), Washington DC -1.04 (n 73, 8.2%); Washington 1.19 (n 72, 29.2%), Montana 1.01 (n 75, 21.3%) and Maine 0.72 (n 86, 18.6%). The model agrees with the prediction for each of these states. For the typical customer these offsets move predicted churn from 0.4% (Hawaii) to 7.5% (Washington). Area code 510 adds a little: -0.32 against -0.45 for area code 408. The West Virginia unit in this part is shut for every training customer (0 rows have it open), so its edge does nothing. ann_87.original: Direct, linear terms for the plans and for international, night and tenure features. An international plan raises predicted churn: a weight of 0.75 per sd, which takes the typical customer from 1.6% to 17.1% (whole model). In the training data the 380 plan holders churned at 42.4% (mean prediction 41.5%), the 3620 others at 11.2%. The voicemail plan and the voicemail message count have weights of opposite sign (-0.98 and 0.80 per sd): self-probe through this part, a plan holder with 0 messages gets -2.29, one with 30 messages -0.51, against -0.06 for a customer without a plan; so the plan lowers predicted churn, most for holders who leave few messages. More international calls lower predicted churn (-0.26 per sd; typical customer 2.1% at 1 call, 0.8% at 10), while international minutes raise it (0.41 per sd). Night minutes add 0.16 per sd and night charge -0.015 per sd. Account length acts through an always-on unit (weight 0.26): the typical customer goes from 1.3% at 1 day to 2.0% at 241 days. Replacing the part by its training mean lowers training AUC from 0.911 to 0.827. The attached formula reproduces the part to within 0.0036.

ann_88.original: The four parts that read daytime usage or service calls, added on the log-odds scale. Together they make predicted churn flat in daytime usage up to about 200 minutes a day and steep above it. Self-probe (typical customer, day charge set to match the minutes, whole model): predicted churn is 1.7% at 100 minutes, 1.6% at 150, 1.5% at 200, 11.2% at 250 and 91.3% at 300. The flat stretch is two parts cancelling: at 150 minutes the service-calls gate gives -0.77 and the day-charge gate 0.98; at 200 minutes they give -0.01 and 0.17. The steep stretch is usage_gate opening: 1.41 at 250 minutes and 4.76 at 300. In the training data the low-usage end sits a little higher and the steep rise is there: mean predicted churn 10.9% below 150 minutes (n 1141, observed 11.9%), 7.7% from 150 to 215 (n 1827, observed 7.9%), 15.4% from 215 to 250 (n 639, observed 14.7%) and 49.6% at 250 or more (n 393, observed 48.9%). Service calls and daytime use add up: see churn_model. Replacing the whole group by its baseline lowers training AUC from 0.911 to 0.696, the largest loss of any part.

ann_89.original: Predicted churn is the logistic function of the sum of the parts' outputs, each with its own weight (attached formula): the parts add on the log-odds scale rather than multiplying one another. The output has no direct input edges of its own: the direct-edge ablation finds 0 of them. The training mean prediction is 14.0% against an observed churn rate of 14.1%; training AUC is 0.911. By ablation the largest parts are usage_and_service (AUC 0.696 without it), account_direct_terms (0.827), service_calls_hinge (0.840) and usage_gate (0.841). Self-probe: the two strongest signals stack. For the typical customer predicted churn is 1.5% with 1 service call and 180 day minutes, 27.4% with 5 calls, 68.6% with 280 minutes, and 92.0% with both. Inputs without connections (the remaining state codes, two area codes and the day, evening and night call counts) do not affect the prediction: the typical customer's prediction is 0.0156, 0.0156 and 0.0156 at 50, 100 and 150 day calls.

parts.name: churn_model
parts.original_hypothesis: Predicted churn is the logistic function of the sum of the parts' outputs, each with its own weight (attached formula): the parts add on the log-odds scale rather than multiplying one another. The output has no direct input edges of its own: the direct-edge ablation finds 0 of them. The training mean prediction is 14.0% against an observed churn rate of 14.1%; training AUC is 0.911. By ablation the largest parts are usage_and_service (AUC 0.696 without it), account_direct_terms (0.827), service_calls_hinge (0.840) and usage_gate (0.841). Self-probe: the two strongest signals stack. For the typical customer predicted churn is 1.5% with 1 service call and 180 day minutes, 27.4% with 5 calls, 68.6% with 280 minutes, and 92.0% with both. Inputs without connections (the remaining state codes, two area codes and the day, evening and night call counts) do not affect the prediction: the typical customer's prediction is 0.0156, 0.0156 and 0.0156 at 50, 100 and 150 day calls.
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: usage_and_service
parts.original_hypothesis: The four parts that read daytime usage or service calls, added on the log-odds scale. Together they make predicted churn flat in daytime usage up to about 200 minutes a day and steep above it. Self-probe (typical customer, day charge set to match the minutes, whole model): predicted churn is 1.7% at 100 minutes, 1.6% at 150, 1.5% at 200, 11.2% at 250 and 91.3% at 300. The flat stretch is two parts cancelling: at 150 minutes the service-calls gate gives -0.77 and the day-charge gate 0.98; at 200 minutes they give -0.01 and 0.17. The steep stretch is usage_gate opening: 1.41 at 250 minutes and 4.76 at 300. In the training data the low-usage end sits a little higher and the steep rise is there: mean predicted churn 10.9% below 150 minutes (n 1141, observed 11.9%), 7.7% from 150 to 215 (n 1827, observed 7.9%), 15.4% from 215 to 250 (n 639, observed 14.7%) and 49.6% at 250 or more (n 393, observed 48.9%). Service calls and daytime use add up: see churn_model. Replacing the whole group by its baseline lowers training AUC from 0.911 to 0.696, the largest loss of any part.

parts.name: service_calls_hinge
parts.original_hypothesis: Customer service calls barely move predicted churn up to 2 calls and then raise it steeply: a hinge. The calls enter twice: a direct term of 1.62 per sd, and a gate (output weight 2.79) that reads the calls with a weight of -0.55 per sd and so shuts when calls are high. While the gate is open it cancels most of the direct slope; once it shuts, the direct slope acts in full. Oregon carries a large negative weight on the gate (-2.65 per sd) and keeps it shut: it is open for 0 of the 84 Oregon training customers. An Oregon customer with few calls therefore gets a lower prediction (1 call, typical case: 0.4% against 1.6%); this looks fitted to those 84 rows. Alaska lowers the gate slightly as well (typical case through this part: -1.16 against -0.30 for Alabama; 56 Alaska customers). In the training data the gate is shut for 1025 customers and open for 2975. The 318 customers with 4 or more calls churned at 50.0% (mean prediction 41.8%); the 3682 with 3 or fewer at 11.1% (mean prediction 11.5%).
